title: Why a violin sounds like a violin

elements.text: Why a violin sounds like a violin

commands.speak: Four strings choose the note — but almost none of the sound you hear comes from them.
A vibrating string is thin, so it slices through the air instead of pushing it — stretched on a rigid frame, it is nearly inaudible.
These are the four open strings: G, D, A and E.
The string only sets the pitch: higher with tension, lower with length and weight.
And the bow never pulls smoothly — the rosin grips the string, drags it sideways, then lets it snap back.
Hermann von Helmholtz worked that motion out in the eighteen-sixties, and the bowed string's grab-and-release still carries his name.
Each snap-back feeds a sawtooth crammed with overtones — a whole ladder of harmonics at once.
That ladder reaches the air by one route only: this little maple wedge.
It rocks sideways with the string and presses the thin spruce belly in and out, hundreds of times a second.
The box breathes through these f-holes, and the air trapped inside rings at a pitch of its own, close to the open D.
Wood and air are loud at some frequencies and dull at others, so certain overtones are boosted and others swallowed.
The string offers every harmonic; the body decides which ones get out.
So the string chooses the note and the box chooses the voice — which is why two violins playing the same note never sound the same.
